erikrose opened PR #14579 from erikrose:interrupt-poll-instruction to bytecodealliance:main:

This is the first step toward implementing MMU-triggered interruption of Wasm (originally suggested in #1749). It's the first little PR broken off the large #12990 for ease of review.

This PR introduces a Cranelift instruction that facilitates resumeable preemptions: in this case, with MMU-based Wasm interruption in mind. However, the same technique is used by HotSpot for stop-the-world GC, so there is potential for other applications.

The original name for this instruction was dead_load_with_context. At the time, that was sufficiently descriptive. However, since then, we've added…

  • Reserving a second register as scratch space for trampolining
  • Returning a new ptr to load from

Thus, it's become specialized enough to the task of implementing virtual-memory-triggered interruption mechanisms that it makes sense to rename it with that in mind.

  • Returning a new ptr to load from

Thus, it's become specialized enough to the task of implementing virtual-memory-triggered interruption mechanisms that it makes sense to rename it with that in mind. Other names I considered include "preempt_poll" (but it ultimately functions cooperatively, so nah), "yield_poll" (too tightly coupled to the one use case I'm chasing right now), and "probe" instead of "poll". HotSpot uses "poll" for their mechanism, so that'll be familiar to some, and it carries a little bit more meaning (repeatedly doing something).

:memo: cfallin submitted PR review:

Thanks -- a bunch of comments on how this is documented/described below (but that's the main task here, to define a clean semantics for the IR operator). Overall shape seems fine.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

"All current backends (x64 and aarch64)" seems wrong here, since Cranelift has more backends than that.

Also I don't think we want to specify details of the register allocation here, unless we want that to become part of the instruction definition/contract.

Finally this description should say more about next_load_ptr's semantics. When resuming, is that pointer then loaded instead? Or is it just the output (defined value) of this instruction, to be used however the user of this instruction wants?

In other words: let's think carefully about defining this as an instruction with well-defined semantics, rather than describing the whole machinery (instruction and its "canonical use") in this one comment.

It might help to define this with pseudocode. Is something like this correct?:

ABI-defined context reg := context
<discard> := memory[load_ptr]
result := ABI-defined next-load-ptr reg

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

Don't say task_switch_trampoline here -- Cranelift should not know or care about (or depend on) the particular way that Wasmtime uses this instruction.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

I'm not sure I understand this comment -- what do you mean by "conceptually flow in the other direction"?

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

Let's fix the indentation here.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

Another thought: to clarify the interface between the different moving parts and decouple the instruction from the use-case, it might help to rename the ABI regs. Maybe "context input" and "context output" (for context and next_load_ptr respectively)?

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

Finally: what do the semantics say about next_load_ptr if the load doesn't trap? Is the value just load_ptr?

So then is it something like this?

ABI-defined context reg := context
ABI-defined next-load-ptr reg := load_ptr
<discard> := memory[load_ptr]
result := ABI-defined next-load-ptr reg

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

Similar comment here as in the aarch64 case.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

This test only tests the IR verifier; let's add compile tests for x64 and aarch64 to lock down the lowerings (so we see if they change/break later) as well.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

Not just "for efficiency" but necessary for the instruction semantics to be coherent, right? Otherwise nothing would write the "result" (defined SSA value) of the instruction in the non-trapping case.
:memo: erikrose submitted PR review.

:speech_balloon: erikrose created PR review comment:

It's an implementation note, attempting to get across that, if the embedder doesn't write anything to x10, next_load_ptr will be identical do it by dint of register pinning.
erikrose updated PR #14579.
:memo: erikrose submitted PR review.

:speech_balloon: erikrose created PR review comment:

"All current backends (x64 and aarch64)" seems wrong here, since Cranelift has more backends than that.

I probably should have said "All current implementations [of this instruction]".

Also I don't think we want to specify details of the register allocation here, unless we want that to become part of the instruction definition/contract.

It's true that we shouldn't name specific registers here in the meta, but the specific registers per ISA are definitely part of the contract; else interrupt handlers wouldn't be able to communicate via context, change the default return value in next_load_ptr, or know which register they could tromp on as scratch space. This is why I added the requirement of the Tail calling convention, as you suggested earlier.

So then is it something like this?

Yes, that last block captures it nicely. By your saying result := the reg and not load_ptr itself, it leaves room for an interrupt handler to scribble on the reg and thus the result.

I've revised my comment to incorporate this concise pseudocode while also preserving the bits about a scratch register and trap table provisions. Let me know what you think.

it might help to rename the ABI regs. Maybe "context input" and "context output" (for context and next_load_ptr respectively)?

Unless you feel very strongly about it, I think "next_load_ptr", in its relationship to "load_ptr", is a useful signal to callers. Both current implementations of the instruction take care to put the result in the same reg as load_ptr, facilitating an efficient polling loop (saving a move) even if the ptr changes sometimes. The current naming leads an attentive reader down that path. (Or at least I intend it to! Maybe it needs more verbiage. As a reader, what do you think?) Of course, callers are always free to use things in unanticipated ways. I've always tried to avoid terms like context, tool, resource, info, data, etc. unless there's really no semantic to reach for.

:thumbs_up: cfallin submitted PR review:

OK, I think this is good to go with the following changes to comments addressed. Thanks for your patience!

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

(And same followup as above: "in the other direction" is extremely unclear and needs to be reworked somehow.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

OK, I still don't get the "flow in the other direction" though. That to me reads like outputs are being copied to inputs, or something like that. (To be clear, my quibble with all of this is unclear/ambiguous writing -- I understand what's going on, but I want to make sure we describe it clearly.)

Why not say "next_load_ptr takes on the value of load_ptr unless a signal handler invoked at the load overwrites it. We constrain next_load_ptr to the same register so this dataflow happens without a move."?

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

s/semantic/semantics/

(In CS/PL lingo at least, we always say "the semantics", which is a mass/uncountable noun, like "the physics" or "the mathematics", and often/usually behaves as a singular -- "the semantics of this operator is ...")
:memo: cfallin submitted PR review.

:speech_balloon: cfallin created PR review comment:

OK, this is fine-ish, I think. It still feels a little prescriptive to me ("this is the one way this instruction must be used" rather than just providing a building block) but it documents everything that needs documenting, I think.
